name: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple
tagline: Famous Muthappan shrine on the Valapattanam — Puthari harvest Thiruvappana in Vrischikam
summary: Riverside Muthappan shrine in Anthoor, Kannur. Known for daily Thiruvappana/theyyam and the Puthari Thiruvappana harvest rite (Vrischikam 16, early December).
description: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple (Parassini Madappura) sits on the banks of the Valapattanam River in Anthoor, Kannur. It is one of North Kerala’s best-known Muthappan centres and a living hub for ritual theyyam and Thiruvappana performances.

The temple matters because it preserves the folk-centred worship of Sree Muthappan — a unique blend of Thiruvappana and Vellattam — where the performer becomes the embodied deity and offerings include ordinary foods and fresh harvest produce.

Visitors find daily ritual performances, a relaxed riverside setting and strong harvest traditions. The temple’s annual Puthari Thiruvappana (the first Thiruvappana of the temple year) celebrates newly harvested rice; farmers and devotees offer puthari (new grain) and share a ceremonial feast.

Practical offerings include regular Thiruvappana/theyyam performances and a temple complex that welcomes devotees and visitors; specific timings, special-event schedules and accommodation details should be confirmed with the temple before travel.
highlights: Daily Thiruvappana/theyyam performances — folk ritual worship unique to North Kerala
Puthari Thiruvappana: harvest offering of new rice (puthari) and ceremonial feast
Riverside location on the Valapattanam River — scenic and peaceful
First Thiruvappana of the temple year (Vrischikam 16) — major local event drawing farmers and devotees

sections.heading: Background
body: Parassinikadavu is the major Parassini Madappura for Muthappan worship in Kannur district. The deity is worshipped through two ritual forms — Thiruvappana (the grand form) and Vellattam (a simpler form) — enacted by performers who answer devotees in a conversational style. The shrine combines folk theyyam practices with temple routines and has long served the surrounding agricultural communities.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a Thiruvappana or Vellattam performance — these are the temple’s central living rituals. Observe offerings, the role of the theyyam performer, and the devotional interaction between performer and public.

If you visit during Puthari Thiruvappana (Vrischikam 16), you will see freshly harvested rice offered to the madappura, Kalasam processions and special evening Vellattam/Thiruvappana performances plus a communal feast prepared from the new crop. This festival marks the agricultural season and is a major local occasion.
Walk the temple grounds by the river for views and local life. Respect ritual spaces and the performers; photography rules vary — confirm on arrival.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: The temple is about 16–20 km from Kannur town (Anthoor/Parassinikadavu area) and is reachable by road from Kannur railway station and Kannur International Airport. The best visiting window for festival atmosphere is late Vrischikam / first week of December when Puthari Thiruvappana is held.

Facilities and exact timings for daily rituals or festival events can change; confirm schedules, special-event dates and any visitor guidance with the temple office or official tourism pages before you travel.

latest.text: Kerala tourism and the temple list Puthari Thiruvappana on Vrischikam 16 (the temple’s first Thiruvappana of the year), which usually falls in the first days of December (commonly December 1 or 2). Confirm exact Gregorian date for 2026 with the temple before travelling.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Vrischikam (mid-November to mid-December) for Puthari; winter months (Nov–Feb) for pleasant weather.
visitorInfo.howToReach: By road from Kannur town (approx 16–20 km). Kannur railway station and Kannur International Airport are the nearest major transport hubs; local buses and taxis serve Parassinikadavu.
etiquette: Puthari offerings are agricultural and communal — bring modest offerings only if invited; observe rather than interrupt rituals.
Ask locally about photography and performer etiquette; theyyam performers are living ritual agents and there are rules around approach.
Festival dates follow the Malayalam calendar (Vrischikam 16); always confirm the temple’s announced Gregorian date for the year.
